summary: This chapter explains what a foodborne illness is, who gets sick most easily, and what kinds of hazards can make food unsafe. A foodborne illness is a disease carried or passed to people by food. When two or more people get the same illness after eating the same food, it is called an outbreak.

Common symptoms are diarrhea, vomiting, fever, nausea, and stomach cramps. Some illnesses, such as Hepatitis A, can also cause jaundice, which means yellow skin and eyes. Older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with weak immune systems get sick more easily and more seriously. Places such as nursing homes, hospitals, and day care centers serve these high-risk groups.

Hazards come in three kinds. Biological hazards are germs such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Chemical hazards are things like cleaners, sanitizers, and pesticides, and metal that moves from a galvanized container into acidic food. Physical hazards are objects such as metal shavings, glass, staples, and bones.

Food most often becomes unsafe through time-temperature abuse, cross-contamination, poor personal hygiene, and poor cleaning and sanitizing. Bacteria grow fastest in moist, low-acid TCS food, such as cooked rice, meat, and cut melons, when it sits in the danger zone. Viruses do not grow in food, but a tiny amount from a sick worker's hands can make people ill, and the FDA names six germs, the Big 6, that spread especially easily.

concepts.definition: A disease carried or passed to people by food. An outbreak is when two or more people get the same illness after eating the same food.
concepts.tip: Outbreak = two or more people, same food.

concepts.definition: Biological (germs such as bacteria and viruses, and toxins they make), chemical (cleaners, sanitizers, pesticides, metal from containers), and physical (objects such as glass, metal, staples, and bones).
concepts.tip: Germ, chemical, or object.

concepts.definition: Older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with weak immune systems (for example, from cancer treatment or HIV). They get sick more easily and more seriously.
concepts.tip: Very young, very old, pregnant, or weak immune system.

concepts.definition: Food that needs time and temperature control for safety because germs grow in it easily. Examples are milk, eggs, meat, poultry, seafood, cooked rice and beans, cut melons, cut tomatoes, cut leafy greens, and sprouts.
concepts.tip: Moist and low in acid usually means TCS.

concepts.definition: The six things bacteria need to grow: Food, Acidity (little or none), Temperature (the danger zone), Time, Oxygen, and Moisture.
concepts.tip: Take away one of them to slow bacteria.

concepts.definition: Six germs the FDA names as spreading easily from sick workers through food: Norovirus, Hepatitis A, Shigella, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, Salmonella Typhi, and nontyphoidal Salmonella.
concepts.tip: Two viruses, Shigella, E. coli, and two kinds of Salmonella.

points: Diarrhea, vomiting, fever, nausea, and cramps are common symptoms; jaundice can point to Hepatitis A.
Viruses do not grow in food; they come from people, so handwashing is the best defense.
Do not keep acidic food such as tomato sauce in galvanized (zinc-coated) containers.
Food must come from an approved, reputable supplier; home-canned food may not be served.
A whole melon is not TCS food, but a cut melon is.

summary: This chapter covers how food handlers keep germs from their own bodies out of food. The main topics are handwashing, gloves, nails and jewelry, work clothes, eating and drinking at work, and what to do when you are sick.

Handwashing is the most important habit. Wet your hands and arms with clean, warm running water, apply soap, scrub for at least 10 to 15 seconds, rinse, and dry with a single-use paper towel or a hand dryer. The whole process takes at least 20 seconds and is done only at a handwashing sink. Wash after using the restroom, touching your hair or face, handling raw meat, taking out garbage, handling chemicals, and eating, drinking, or smoking. Hand sanitizer can be used only after washing, never in place of it.

Ready-to-eat food must not be touched with bare hands, even right after washing; use single-use gloves, tongs, or deli tissue. Single-use gloves are thrown away and never washed or reused, and they are changed when dirty or torn, between tasks, and after raw meat before ready-to-eat food. Keep nails short and clean, and wear nail polish or artificial nails only with intact gloves. Cover a cut on the hand with a bandage and a glove. Wear a hair restraint, and on the hands and arms wear no jewelry except a plain band ring.

Tell your manager if you have vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, a sore throat with fever, or an infected cut, or if a doctor diagnoses one of the Big 6 illnesses. A worker with vomiting or diarrhea is excluded (kept out of the operation) and can usually return after 24 hours without symptoms. A sore throat with fever means restriction (kept away from open food) in most places, but exclusion where a high-risk group is served, such as a nursing home.

concepts.definition: Wet hands and arms with warm running water, apply soap, scrub at least 10 to 15 seconds, rinse, and dry with a single-use paper towel or hand dryer. The whole process takes at least 20 seconds.
concepts.tip: Scrub 10 to 15 seconds, whole process at least 20.

concepts.definition: Ready-to-eat food (food that will not be cooked again) must not be touched with bare hands. Use single-use gloves, tongs, spatulas, or deli tissue.
concepts.tip: Washing your hands is not enough for ready-to-eat food.

concepts.definition: Gloves used for one task and then thrown away. Change them when dirty or torn, when you start a new task, after an interruption, and after raw meat before ready-to-eat food. Wash your hands before putting on new gloves.
concepts.tip: Never wash or reuse single-use gloves.

concepts.definition: A liquid or gel used on hands only after correct handwashing. It does not replace washing, and it does not replace gloves or utensils for ready-to-eat food.
concepts.tip: Wash first, sanitize second.

concepts.definition: Restriction keeps a sick worker away from open food and clean equipment, but they may do other work. Exclusion keeps the worker out of the operation completely.
concepts.tip: Restrict = no food contact. Exclude = do not come in.

concepts.definition: Vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice (yellow skin or eyes), a sore throat with fever, and an infected cut or sore with pus on the hands, wrists, or arms. Also report a doctor's diagnosis of a Big 6 illness.
concepts.tip: Vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice: report and stay out.

points: Wash hands only in a handwashing sink, never in a prep, dish, or mop sink.
On the hands and arms, the only jewelry allowed while prepping food is a plain band ring.
Nail polish or artificial nails are allowed only with intact gloves.
Eat, drink, and smoke only in set-aside areas away from food; a drink in a prep area needs a lid and straw.
Vomiting or diarrhea: excluded; usually back after 24 hours without symptoms.
Sore throat with fever: restricted in most places, excluded where a high-risk group is served.

compare.title: Restriction vs. exclusion

Kept out of the operation completely
Sore throat with fever in most places
Vomiting, diarrhea, new jaundice; sore throat with fever at a nursing home

summary: This chapter covers two ways food can be made unsafe by other food: cross-contamination, when germs move from one food or surface to another, and allergen cross-contact, when an allergen gets into food that should not have it. Both are prevented by keeping foods apart and by cleaning and sanitizing between tasks.

To prevent cross-contamination, store ready-to-eat food above raw meat, seafood, and poultry. The shelf order follows cooking temperature, from top to bottom: ready-to-eat food, seafood, whole cuts of beef and pork, ground meat and ground fish, and poultry on the bottom. Use separate cutting boards and tools for raw and ready-to-eat food, or prepare them at different times and wash, rinse, and sanitize in between. Scoop ice with a clean scoop stored outside the ice, never with a glass.

The FDA lists nine major food allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. Signs of a reaction include hives, swelling of the lips, face, or throat, and trouble breathing. Trouble breathing and throat swelling can mean a severe reaction, so call 911 right away.

To prevent cross-contact, tell the kitchen about every allergy order and mark it clearly. Wash your hands, change gloves, and use cleaned and sanitized tools before making an allergy order. Do not cook allergy orders in fryer oil shared with allergens, because heat does not destroy allergens. If an allergen gets into a dish by mistake, throw it away and make a new one; picking it off is not enough.

concepts.definition: Germs moving from one food or surface to another, such as from raw chicken to a cutting board and then to lettuce.
concepts.tip: Separate, or clean and sanitize in between.

concepts.definition: From top to bottom: ready-to-eat food, seafood, whole cuts of beef and pork, ground meat and ground fish, then poultry. Foods that need a higher cooking temperature go lower.
concepts.tip: Poultry (165°F) always goes on the bottom.

source.org: ServSafe Food Handler course (National Restaurant Association)

concepts.definition: When an allergen gets into food that should not have it, for example from shared tools, gloves, or fryer oil.
concepts.tip: Cross-contact is about allergens; cross-contamination is about germs.

concepts.definition: Milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. Sesame was added in 2023.
concepts.tip: Crustaceans are shrimp, crab, and lobster, not clams or oysters.

source.org: U.S. FDA (Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act, FASTER Act)

concepts.definition: Signs include hives or an itchy rash, swelling of the lips, face, or throat, wheezing or trouble breathing, and stomach cramps, vomiting, or diarrhea. A severe reaction can cause death.
concepts.tip: Trouble breathing: call 911 at once.

points: Ready-to-eat food goes above raw meat, seafood, and poultry; raw poultry goes on the bottom shelf.
After raw meat, wash, rinse, and sanitize a cutting board before using it for ready-to-eat food.
Prepare raw and ready-to-eat food at different times if they must share a work area.
Use a clean ice scoop stored outside the ice; never scoop with a glass.
Heat does not destroy allergens, so do not use shared fryer oil for allergy orders.
If an allergen gets into a dish by mistake, remake it; never pick the allergen off.

compare.title: Cross-contamination vs. cross-contact
rows: Raw chicken juice on a salad
Peanut butter on a knife used for a nut-free sandwich
Cooking can kill some germs, but ready-to-eat food is not cooked again
No, heat does not destroy allergens

summary: This chapter is about keeping food out of the temperature range where germs grow fastest. You will learn which foods need extra care, how to use a thermometer, and the safe temperatures and times for receiving, storing, thawing, cooking, holding, cooling, and reheating food. Many test questions use these numbers, so they are worth learning well.

Germs grow fastest between 41°F and 135°F, which is called the temperature danger zone. Foods that need time and temperature control to stay safe are called TCS foods. They include meat, poultry, fish, milk, eggs, cooked rice and beans, baked potatoes, and cut melons, tomatoes, and leafy greens. To check temperatures, put the thermometer in the thickest part of the food. Clean and sanitize it before and after use, and calibrate it with the ice-point method so it reads 32°F in ice water.

Receive and hold cold TCS food at 41°F or lower, and hold hot TCS food at 135°F or higher. Thaw food in the refrigerator, under running drinkable water at 70°F or lower, in a microwave if you cook it right away, or as part of cooking. Never thaw food on the counter. Cook poultry and stuffing to 165°F, ground meat to 155°F for 17 seconds, fish and whole cuts like steaks and chops to 145°F for 15 seconds, and fruits and vegetables for hot holding to 135°F.

Cool hot food from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F or lower within the next 4 hours, for 6 hours in all. Reheat food for hot holding to 165°F within 2 hours. Ready-to-eat TCS food kept at 41°F or lower can be stored for up to 7 days, and the day it was made counts as day 1. Food held with time as the control instead of temperature must be served or thrown out within 4 hours.

concepts.definition: The range from 41°F to 135°F, where germs that cause foodborne illness grow fastest.
concepts.tip: Cold at 41°F or lower, hot at 135°F or higher.

concepts.definition: Time/Temperature Control for Safety food. Moist, protein-rich, or cut foods that let germs grow, such as meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, cooked rice, and cut melons, tomatoes, and leafy greens.
concepts.tip: If it is moist and was cooked or cut, think TCS.

concepts.definition: Put the stem in a container of ice and water and wait for the reading to stop moving. It should read 32°F. If it does not, adjust it. Calibrate after a drop or a big temperature change.
concepts.tip: Ice water = 32°F.

concepts.definition: Poultry and stuffing: 165°F (less than 1 second). Ground meat: 155°F for 17 seconds. Fish, steaks, and chops: 145°F for 15 seconds. Fruits and vegetables for hot holding: 135°F.
concepts.tip: 165 poultry, 155 ground, 145 whole cuts and fish, 135 vegetables.

concepts.definition: Cool from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then from 70°F to 41°F or lower within the next 4 hours. If food misses the 2-hour mark, reheat it to 165°F and cool again, or throw it out.
concepts.tip: 2 hours + 4 hours = 6 hours.

concepts.definition: Ready-to-eat TCS food made in-house and kept at 41°F or lower can be stored for up to 7 days. Label it with the use-by date. The day it is made is day 1.
concepts.tip: Made on the 4th: last day is the 10th.

concepts.term: Time as a public health control
concepts.definition: Holding food without temperature control. The food must be labeled with a throw-out time and be served or thrown out within 4 hours.
concepts.tip: Out of hot holding at 10:30 a.m. means gone by 2:30 p.m.

points: Danger zone: 41°F to 135°F.
Receive and hold cold TCS food at 41°F or lower; hold hot food at 135°F or higher.
Check temperature in the thickest part of the food.
Safe thawing: refrigerator, running water at 70°F or lower, microwave (cook right away), or as part of cooking.
Reheat for hot holding to 165°F within 2 hours, on cooking equipment, not in a steam table.
Cool in shallow pans or an ice-water bath, never on the counter or in a deep covered pot.

summary: This chapter explains how to keep surfaces, dishes, and the whole building clean and safe. You will learn the difference between cleaning and sanitizing, when to do both, how to use a three-compartment sink, how to handle chemicals, and how to keep garbage and pests under control.

Cleaning removes food and dirt from a surface. Sanitizing reduces germs on a clean surface to safe levels. The order is clean, rinse, sanitize, and air-dry. Clean and sanitize a food-contact surface after you use it, before you work with a different type of food, after an interruption that may have contaminated it, and at least every 4 hours if it is in constant use.

At a three-compartment sink, scrape food off first. Then wash in detergent, rinse in clean water, sanitize, and let items air-dry. Never towel-dry sanitized items. Change the sanitizer when it is dirty or weak, and check it with a test kit. Keep wet wiping cloths in sanitizer solution between uses, and store clean dishes dry, off the floor, and upside down.

Store chemicals in a separate area, away from and never above food. Label any working container with the chemical's common name, never mix chemicals, and use the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) to learn about dangers and first aid. Remove garbage from prep areas often and keep containers covered. If you see signs of pests, such as droppings, gnaw marks, nests, or a strong oily smell, tell your manager. Only a licensed pest control operator should apply pesticides.

concepts.definition: Cleaning removes food and dirt. Sanitizing reduces germs on a clean surface to safe levels. Sanitizer does not work well on a dirty surface.
concepts.tip: Clean first, then sanitize.

concepts.definition: After using a surface, before working with a different type of food, after an interruption, and at least every 4 hours for items in constant use.
concepts.tip: Constant use: every 4 hours.

concepts.definition: Scrape, then wash in detergent, rinse in clean water, sanitize, and air-dry. Change the sanitizer when it is dirty and check it with a test kit.
concepts.tip: Scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, air-dry.

concepts.definition: Keep chemicals in a separate area away from food and prep areas, and never above food. Label working containers with the chemical's common name. Never mix chemicals.
concepts.tip: Chemicals go away from and below food.

concepts.definition: A sheet from the chemical's maker that explains its dangers, safe use and storage, and first aid if someone is exposed.
concepts.tip: SDS = safety and first aid for a chemical.

concepts.definition: Droppings, gnaw marks, nests, egg cases, a strong oily smell, and live or dead pests. Report them to your manager. A licensed pest control operator should apply pesticides.
concepts.tip: See it, report it; do not spray it yourself.

points: Never towel-dry sanitized dishes or surfaces; let them air-dry.
Do not stack dishes while they are still wet.
Keep wet wiping cloths in sanitizer solution between uses.
Dump mop water only in a service (mop) sink.
Remove garbage from prep areas often and keep containers covered.
Store clean dishes and utensils at least 6 inches off the floor.
